label: Adjacency and weighted degree
assumptions: Declare whether rows encode outgoing edges.
Weights are nonnegative for a random-walk interpretation.
derivation: Place each edge weight at its row and column. Summing a row counts outgoing weight; this is bookkeeping, not an inferred relationship.
example: A unit-weight path of three vertices has degrees (1,2,1) when represented as an undirected graph.
limitations: A directed graph generally has different incoming and outgoing degree.

label: Combinatorial Laplacian
assumptions: Undirected graph with nonnegative weights.
derivation: Row i acts on x by summing w_ij(x_i-x_j); a constant signal produces zero differences.
example: For the three-vertex path, L=[[1,-1,0],[-1,2,-1],[0,-1,1]], with eigenvalues 0,1,3.
limitations: L is singular on each connected component. A directed version needs a separately stated convention.

label: Dirichlet quadratic form
assumptions: Symmetric nonnegative weights.
The double sum counts both orientations.
derivation: Expand the square and collect the two degree terms; symmetry turns both into x^TDx, while cross terms give twice x^TAx.
example: For path values (1,0,-1), the two undirected edge differences both equal 1, hence x^TLx=2.
limitations: Units are weight times signal squared. Calling this physical energy requires an additional physical model.

label: Grounded Poisson problem
assumptions: Every connected component of interior vertices reaches a fixed boundary.
Boundary values and compatible source units are specified.
derivation: Partition Lu=b into interior and boundary blocks; move the known boundary term to the right. The grounded interior operator is positive definite under the connectivity assumption.
example: For a three-point path with endpoints 1 and 0 and no interior source, 2u_middle=1, so u_middle=0.5.
limitations: Without grounding or compatibility constraints, inversion is not unique or may be inconsistent.

label: Graph heat flow

variables.unit: inverse time when L is dimensionless

assumptions: Fixed symmetric nonnegative graph.
Linear dynamics.
derivation: Diagonalize L=UΛUᵀ; each mode obeys a scalar decay equation with solution exp(-κλt).
example: A mode with λ=2 and κ=1 s^-1 decays to exp(-2)≈0.1353 of its initial amplitude after 1 s.
limitations: Smoothing can remove a rare but essential distinction. A diffusion parameter is not automatically a biological timescale.

label: Graph wave modes
assumptions: A physical or simulated second-order dynamical law is explicitly posited.
L is positive semidefinite.
derivation: Project onto each eigenvector to obtain an independent harmonic-oscillator equation.
example: For path eigenvalue λ=3 and ω0=2 rad/s, the mode has ω=2√3 rad/s.
limitations: A note graph alone has no clock, mass, stiffness, or measured acoustic frequency.

label: Row-stochastic transition
assumptions: Nonnegative weights.
A separate redistribution rule is defined for dangling rows.
derivation: Divide each outgoing weight by the row sum, producing total probability one.
example: Weights (2,1) yield outgoing probabilities (2/3,1/3).
limitations: Negative relations cannot be inserted as negative probabilities. Keep contradicts as a separate semantic channel.

label: Personalized PageRank
assumptions: P is row-stochastic after dangling-node handling.
s is nonnegative and sums to one.
derivation: At a fixed point, collect terms in p. Invertibility follows because the spectral radius of αPᵀ is below one. The Neumann series sums walks of every length with geometric damping.
example: For two alternating vertices, seed (1,0), and α=0.85, p=(1/1.85,0.85/1.85)≈(0.54054,0.45946).
limitations: Stationary mass measures graph affinity. It is not probability that a scientific claim is correct.

label: PageRank residual bound
assumptions: Stochastic transition with 0≤α<1.
derivation: The future increments are bounded by a geometric sequence. Sum their norms to bound the distance from the current iterate to the limit.
example: At α=0.85 and residual 10^-10, this bound is at most 6.67×10^-10.
limitations: An iteration cap can stop before this bound is small; record residual and iteration count.

label: Positive inverse document frequency
assumptions: Compute statistics only over authorized active documents.
Natural logarithm is used.
derivation: The smoothed frequency ratio increases as a term becomes rarer; the outer 1 keeps this common BM25 variant positive.
limitations: Changing the corpus changes IDF. It does not measure the truth or novelty of a claim.

label: BM25 retrieval score
assumptions: Chosen tokenizer and document construction are fixed.
Implementation uses k1=1.2 and b=0.75.
derivation: The fractional term grows with term frequency but saturates. Length normalization changes the denominator according to relative document length.
example: If a document has average length and term frequency 1, the fraction equals 1, leaving exactly its IDF contribution.
limitations: These constants are a baseline, not optimized for this corpus. Repeated labels receive deliberate extra weight.

label: Cosine similarity
assumptions: Both vectors have nonzero norm.
Both come from the same compatible embedding space.
derivation: Divide the inner product by magnitudes to isolate the angle between vectors.
example: Vectors (1,0) and (1,1) have cosine 1/√2≈0.7071.
limitations: High similarity can link incompatible claims. Embeddings are a documented future adapter, not used in the implemented baseline.

label: Weighted reciprocal rank fusion

variables.meaning: one-based rank in retrieval channel j

assumptions: Missing items contribute zero.
Ranks start at one.
derivation: Replace incomparable raw scores with reciprocal rank contributions, then sum channels. The implemented weights are 1 for lexical and 0.7 for graph, with c=60.
example: An item ranked first in both channels scores 1.7/61≈0.027869; this is a ranking score, not 2.79% confidence.
limitations: Weights need held-out evaluation; a dense graph can still introduce irrelevant linked items.

label: Relevance and redundancy tradeoff
assumptions: Comparable, bounded relevance and similarity scales.
derivation: A greedy step rewards query relevance and penalizes similarity to selected evidence. This defines an engineering policy rather than a general optimum.
example: At λ=0.7, relevance 0.9 and maximum redundancy 0.8 give 0.63-0.24=0.39.
limitations: Not implemented in the initial retrieval core; retained as an evaluable extension.

label: Shannon entropy of a declared distribution
assumptions: A normalized distribution and outcome space are specified.
Use 0 log 0=0 by continuity.
derivation: Weight each outcome's self-information by its probability. This measures uncertainty of that distribution, not semantic wisdom.
example: A fair binary variable has entropy 1 bit; a deterministic variable has entropy 0.
limitations: Low entropy may reflect unwarranted certainty. It is not evidence quality.

label: Expected local cache latency
assumptions: Hit and miss latencies include the same measurement boundaries.
Workload hit fraction is representative.
derivation: Condition total expectation on the two disjoint cases. If miss cost is measured after lookup instead, add the lookup cost separately.
example: With h=0.8, a 2 ms hit and a 40 ms complete miss, E[T]=9.6 ms.
limitations: Mean latency does not describe p95 or concurrent queueing. These numbers are an example, not a measured product result.

label: Two-level average memory access time
assumptions: Each lower-tier cost is incurred only after an upper-tier miss.
Use incremental costs, not complete inclusive timings.
derivation: Expand a decision tree: every request pays T1, m1 of requests pay T2, and m1m2 pay T3.
example: T1=1, T2=10, T3=100, m1=0.1, m2=0.2 yield 4 time units.
limitations: Correlated workloads and overlapping asynchronous fetches require a different timing model.

label: Poisson-update freshness model
assumptions: Updates are modeled as a homogeneous Poisson process.
derivation: The no-update probability is the zero-count Poisson mass exp(-λt); subtract from one.
example: With λ=1 update/hour and age 0.5 hour, probability of an intervening update is about 0.3935.
limitations: Real source changes are often bursty or adversarial. Versioned invalidation is stronger than this heuristic.

label: Fully associative LRU hit condition

variables.meaning: distinct other items since previous access

assumptions: Fully associative LRU.
Uniform-sized entries and no external invalidation.
First use has infinite reuse distance.
derivation: Every distinct intervening item moves the reused entry down one position in the recency stack; capacity C retains the first C positions.
example: Trace A,B,C,A has reuse distance 2 for the last A: it misses at capacity 2 and hits at capacity 3.
limitations: The supplied persisted cache is FIFO and does not claim this LRU guarantee.

label: Complete cache dependency key
assumptions: Canonical serialization is deterministic.
All output-relevant dependencies are included.
Cryptographic hash collisions are assumed negligible.
derivation: Treat the result as a function of declared inputs. Equal keys justify reuse only insofar as the serialization captures every relevant input.
example: A source URL correction changes V and therefore the key even when the node summary text is unchanged.
limitations: A digest does not validate the source, authenticate a caller, or prove semantic equivalence.

label: Evidence selection under a byte budget
assumptions: Utilities and sizes are specified.
Independent additive utility is an approximation.
derivation: A constrained subset problem formalizes why not every retrieved item fits. The implementation greedily tries ranked packets and checks actual UTF-8 bytes.
example: With sizes 6 and 5 and budget 5, only the second item fits, regardless of the first item's better rank.
limitations: Greedy rank order does not solve general knapsack optimally; correlated evidence requires nonadditive utility.

label: Traversal complexity
assumptions: Adjacency lists and a visited set.
Constant-time set operations are an average-case assumption.
derivation: Each vertex enters the queue once and each relevant adjacency is examined a bounded number of times.
example: In a cycle A→B→C→A, the visited set stops the fourth enqueue of A.
limitations: Building the eligible subgraph and adjacency has its own whole-graph cost; report that in end-to-end benchmarks.

label: DAG topological condition
assumptions: Remove vertices of zero indegree and their outgoing edges.
derivation: A finite acyclic directed graph has a zero-indegree vertex. A cycle leaves each of its vertices with an incoming edge, preventing complete elimination.
example: A requires B and B requires A gives no valid topological order; C depending on A can also remain blocked.
limitations: Remaining blocked vertices are not necessarily all members of a cycle.

label: Simple Hebbian weight construction
assumptions: A specified binary-pattern associative model.
This is a theoretical rule, not a universal synaptic law.
derivation: Correlated components contribute positive weights and opposite components negative weights; summing patterns superposes their associations.
example: For one pattern (1,-1), the off-diagonal weights are -1/2 under N=2 normalization.
limitations: Interference and spurious attractors occur. Coactivation does not imply causal evidence.

label: Binary Hopfield Lyapunov function
assumptions: W=Wᵀ and diagonal zero.
Asynchronous single-unit updates align with the local field.
derivation: If only state i changes, ΔE=-(s_i'−s_i)(Σ_j W_ij s_j−θ_i). Choosing the state aligned with the field makes this nonpositive.
example: Two positively coupled units lower this function by agreeing rather than disagreeing, for zero thresholds.
limitations: Synchronous updates can oscillate. The function is not automatically a joule-valued physical energy.

label: Scaled dot-product attention
assumptions: Matrix dimensions are compatible.
Softmax operates across available keys, with any mask explicitly stated.
derivation: Dot products give compatibility logits; scaling moderates their growth with dimension, softmax normalizes, and the resulting weights mix values.
example: For two equal unmasked logits, each value receives weight 1/2.
limitations: A KV cache stores intermediate tensors; it is different from external source-linked memory.

label: Exponential retrieval-priority heuristic
assumptions: A software prioritization rule is explicitly chosen.
derivation: Solve dw/dt=−w/τ. This defines a convenient recency prior; it is not fitted biological evidence.
example: After time τ, weight is w0/e≈0.3679w0.
limitations: Never let an arbitrary decay delete provenance or turn an established theorem false.

label: Evidence precision and recall
assumptions: Gold relevance and evidence units are specified.
Define behavior for empty denominators before evaluation.
derivation: Precision asks how much retrieved evidence is relevant; recall asks how much relevant evidence was found.
example: Retrieving 5 items, 3 relevant, from 4 relevant items gives precision 0.6 and recall 0.75.
limitations: Gold labels can be incomplete; duplicate passages must not inflate independent support.

label: Discounted cumulative gain

variables.meaning: ideal score under the same labels

assumptions: Nonnegative relevance grades.
Define the all-zero relevance case.
derivation: Higher-ranked relevant items contribute more. Divide by the best available ordering to normalize the score.
example: For binary relevance (1,0,1), DCG@3=1+0+1/2=1.5.
limitations: Metric choice does not certify answer correctness or source trustworthiness.

label: Brier calibration score
assumptions: A well-defined population of binary outcomes.
Predictions precede observed outcomes.
derivation: Use the squared error of probabilistic predictions and average over evaluated cases.
example: Predictions (0.8,0.2) for outcomes (1,0) have Brier score 0.04.
limitations: Graph ranks and RRF scores are not probabilities and must not be inserted directly as calibrated confidence.

label: Measured improvement in a fixed loop
assumptions: Hold evaluation data and judging procedure fixed within a comparison.
Track resource cost and regressions separately.
derivation: Evaluate both revisions on the same criterion, then subtract. This distinguishes observed progress from activity counts.
example: Recall increasing from 0.60 to 0.65 is a five-percentage-point change on that evaluation; it is not proof of universal improvement.
limitations: Repeated tuning on the same cases can overfit; retain held-out questions and report uncertainty.
